title: A Shameless Valley
text:
For 11 days this month, Silicon Valley gave the impression that it would finally, against all odds, subject itself to a genuine moment of shame. First, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having cheated on his wife with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of being a spy, putting his company, the AI industry it undergirds, and the nation’s security at risk. He apologized profusely. Then it was reported that Huang had had another affair, this one with an Nvidia executive, and he resigned. It seemed that one of Silicon Valley’s titans was facing a reckoning.

 But late last night, Donald Trump posted on Truth Social, “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang.” This outcome, the president wrote , “would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” Those words were evidently as much a command as they were a wish. This morning, Nvidia’s board of directors announced that it had unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as CEO. The president then posted a meme that, even for him, was grotesque: a seemingly AI-generated image of Huang, face bloodied from a wound, raising a fist clenching a red brassiere with an Nvidia flag waving in the background—modeled, of course, on the photo taken just after the first assassination attempt on Trump. So much for shame.

 [ Read:A ] $5.7 Trillion Face-Plant 

 It’s worth underscoring just how damning Huang’s scandals were. He admitted to having a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman tied to a company that was suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China—thereby sidestepping U.S. export controls—at the same time that he was lobbying tirelessly to ease restrictions meant to keep American chips out of the hands of Chinese competition. For a company in Nvidia’s position, it was an earth-shattering revelation: Nvidia essentially has a monopoly on the chips used to train the most advanced AI models. That has made the firm spectacularly wealthy—earlier this year, it was valued at a record $5.7 trillion. Huang, in turn, used that wealth to underwrite much of the AI economy, funding all manner of data centers and start-ups as a sort of financial backstop. Huang’s resignation was followed by one of the worst weeks on Wall Street in recent memory. Further reports since his resignation—of a third affair and an abusive management style—only made Huang come off worse. A similar scandal in almost any other industry would result in universal political condemnation and an attempt, by both the company and its peers, to distance themselves from the disgraced former executive.

 But it’s just the opposite here. The New York Times has reported that Trump and Vice President Vance spent the weekend pushing Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang. Almost immediately after this morning’s announcement, Trump posted on Truth Social to celebrate “the correct and proper” decision to restore Huang, a “Great Patriot and National Treasure.”

 The mood in Silicon Valley is ebullient: The company’s stock jumped by more than 30 percent on the news, and investors and tech executives have erupted in an ovation. “The wisdom of the crowd prevails,” the hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman wrote on X. Elon Musk, a vocal Huang supporter, added : “The mistake has been corrected.” Many of Silicon Valley’s most powerful characters seem vindicated—after all, they downplayed and dismissed Huang’s follies as simple mistakes and aberrations.

 In fact, the whole thing—recklessness and scandal followed by impunity—is the norm in the tech world. Silicon Valley has developed a reputation for generosity and forgiveness when it comes to its own sins. Musk has appeared to endorse racist and xenophobic conspiracy theories but sits on a multitrillion-dollar empire of businesses. Meta has been credibly accused of fueling ethnic violence, enabling the spread of misinformation, and harming children through addictive product design—the latter for which it agreed to a major settlement this summer—but remains among the largest companies in the world, and is structured such that Mark Zuckerberg basically cannot be fired. Almost exactly three years ago, Sam Altman was fired from OpenAI for being “not consistently candid” with the firm’s board of directors, only to be reinstated within days after Microsoft and other major investors rallied behind him. Now the entire AI industry is rushing headlong to build products that are jeopardizing the internet as we know it and, per AI executives’ own warnings, could destroy the planet. Meanwhile, Anthropic employees, post–public offering, are estimated to be worth more than the bottom third of U.S. households.

 Over the past week and a half, legions of tech CEOs came out in support of Huang. “America needs to have more Jensens,” Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas said last Monday. This morning, the investor Chamath Palihapitiya wrote on X that Nvidia’s decision “prevented a massive economic own goal.” Just business as usual for some of the wealthiest companies in the world. (Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) Altman, asked last week about whether he thought Huang should return, demurred but said he felt “personal strong empathy” for his (soon-to-be) fellow ex-ex-CEO. This morning, Altman posted a single word: “Jensen!”

 Huang’s return underscores the most important and perhaps singular value driving Silicon Valley: winning. Today that means more chips and data centers, more powerful AI models, greater revenues, soaring stock prices and valuations. Integrity, candor, atonement, and consequences seem like secondary concerns. The repercussions of the industry’s failures—wild swings in the stock market, technologies that wreak havoc on other industries and individual lives, a corrosion of cultural decency—are for everyone else to manage. Personal victory also happens to be one of the president’s major motivations. Trump has aligned himself with every tech CEO he deems successful—Altman, Apple’s Tim Cook, and most of all Huang, who is once again arguably the most influential CEO in the world.

 Earlier this year, in a now infamous interview, Huang said that “you’re not talking to somebody who woke up a loser.” Today, Silicon Valley decided to embrace its once and future king, whatever mistakes he made. After just 11 days of losing, Huang woke up winning once again.
